As <term>Ptolemy</term> <gloss>Greek astronomer and astrologer</gloss> says, when he arrives at the place of any star, he stirs up the force that it has in the air. For instance, with <term>Mars</term> he disposes heat, and with <term>Saturn</term> he disposes cold and the very spirit and mind of man. Hence it is said by <term>Homer</term> and proven by <term>Aristotle</term> that there are such motions in the mind as the Sun, the prince and moderator of the planets, brings forth on individual days.

The Moon, however, being nearest to the earth, is the receptacle of all celestial influence. By the speed of her course, she is joined each month to the Sun and the remaining planets and stars. Having become, as it were, the wife of all the stars, the most fertile of stars, she receives the rays and influences of the Sun and the other planets and stars as if they were a fetus, and brings them forth as if giving birth to the inferior world near her. For all the stars pour themselves into her, she being the final recipient, who then communicates the influences of all the superiors to the inferiors and pours them back upon the earth. She disposes these inferior things more manifestly than the others, and her motion is more sensible due to the familiarity and proximity she has with us. Being a medium between the superiors and the inferiors, she communicates to all these things. Therefore, her motion is to be observed before the others, as if she were the parent of all conceptions, which she unfolds in various ways to these inferior things, according to her varied complexion, motion, position, and different aspects to the planets and other stars. And although she may receive powers from all the stars, she is especially filled with a life-giving virtue from the Sun whenever she is conjoined to him, and she borrows a complexion according to his intuition. For in the first quarter, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <gloss>followers of Aristotle</gloss> report, she is hot and moist; in the second, hot and dry; in the third, cold and dry; and in the fourth, cold and moist. And although she is the lowest of the stars, she nevertheless unfolds all the conceptions of the superiors. For from her, in the celestial realm, begins the series of things which <term>Plato</term> calls the <term>golden chain</term> <gloss>an ontological hierarchy connecting the divine to the material</gloss>, by which each thing, either connected to another or a cause, depends upon the superior until one reaches the supreme cause of all, from which all things depend. Hence it is that without this intermediate Moon, we are entirely unable to draw the power of the superiors. Whence <term>Thebit</term> <gloss>Thabit ibn Qurra, astronomer</gloss> commands that, to capture the virtue of any star, one must take the stone and herb of that star when the Moon either happily enters or happily beholds the same star.

# LIB. XI. ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.

<margin>Chap. VIII. The foolish machinations of the Rabbis.</margin>
...so they tolerate it, lest in their own time they pay for this rashness by being suspended from a golden rope.

Not long ago, a small book was sent to me, written in the Hebrew language, most full of the secrets of Nature, or more truly, of lies. In it, among other things, a herb was described, by the name of *Boriza*, by which any metal whatever could be converted into gold, so that foolish Rabbi asserted. But since the matter is worthy of note, I append the ridiculous operation, from which it will appear with what incongruous things these sycophants of this flour <note>a metaphor for "of this ilk" or "this brand of liar"</note> are accustomed to deceive men. Thus he says: <term>הוריזא היא עשב שמה לונאריא</term> <gloss>Boriza is a herb, the name of which is Lunaria.</gloss> But omitting the Hebrew words as they are rather long, let us put forth the interpretation itself: Hear therefore and laugh, <term>Reader</term>, at the foolish promises. Put the juice of this herb into silver, and make it boil in this juice, and it will become a red broth; from this make a powder, which, when cast upon copper, will change it into gold, and one ounce of this powder is sufficient to convert one hundred ounces of copper into gold. This herb is born at springs and rivers and on high mountains, as I believe, more truly in Utopia. It has a red and violet stalk, and it has milk within, and it will become copper. (O great profit!) And if you put some of this upon lead, gold will come; the juice of this herb placed upon iron will become silver, and the powder of this herb placed upon silver will make gold, and if you place it in urine with spikenard, and drink one ounce daily, it will transmute the old into the young. But let us leave these foolish machinations of the Cabalists to be refuted not by Philosophers, but by delirious little women.

I could bring forward here innumerable examples from the solemn frauds of the Arabs, which are found everywhere in their books on the minerals of Nature and are brought in regarding gold-making. But since they are unworthy to be related, I have deemed them to be suppressed by silence.

# C H A P T E R  IX.
# That the demon for the most part mixes himself with the cultivators of Alchemy.

<margin>Chap. IX. The love of gold drags men into destruction.</margin>
<margin>In what ways Satan deceives those desirous of gold.</margin>
St. Paul said very truly in his Epistle to Timothy, ch. 6, v. 9: <quote>Those who want to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge men into ruin and perdition: for the love of money is the root of all evils, which some by desiring have wandered from the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows.</quote> It is so. The immoderate desire for riches is the net of the evil demon, by which, as of old, so even to this day, it does not cease to drag a great part of the human race into the final ruin of their souls. Since there is nothing in human affairs that is sought with greater desire, or upon which more anxiety is expended, than the accumulation of treasures; for innumerable examples teach us that by their possession and unjust usurpation, the door has been opened to every kind of vice and crime: while those who are powerful in riches can obtain whatever they wish, whether it be power, or the ambition of honors and the acquisition of dignities, or a worldly life swelling with pride and filled with the other delights of the flesh. Hence it is no wonder that <term>Alchemy</term>, the only most fallacious promiser of such riches, is esteemed so highly and is sought after with such anxious study by all men of whatever condition they may be. The enemy of the human race is not ignorant of this burning thirst for gold, whence he attacks unwary mortals with arts all the more dangerous the more hidden they are. It happens, therefore, that because they gape for gold with too great a desire, and are for the most part hindered by insurmountable difficulties which occur in the Great Art, with all hope of attaining the art removed; when, nevertheless, anxious between hope and fear, they apply themselves more solicitously to the coveted possession of riches, at length driven headlong by despair, they either seek out the discovery of treasures or, summoned by the magical arts of the evil demon, they implore his help in perfecting the art; and thus, finally bound by a Satanic pact, they fall into every abyss of impiety, and without any fruit, they conclude their life with a miserable end. I have known many deceived by such illusions as these, especially those students of more curious learning, who without previous examination, without light, unconsulted, and with a completely rash daring, embraced the vanity of <term>Alchemy</term>, and by the just judgment of GOD, deceived by the devil, they perished in a thousand precipices of errors; for how dear it is to the demon to attack men with similar arts, we have demonstrated most amply in <term>Oedipus, Part 1, On Idolatry</term>. For not only do demons mix themselves secretly in those mockeries of magical arts, but also in all vain and false insanities, such as Astrology, which gets its origin from these things, and divinatory and cabalistic arts, and all those species which have the name <term>μαντεία</term> <gloss>divination</gloss>, with which they circumvent the curious with excessive credulity, so much so that those who neglect to watch against their deceits vanish in their thoughts, and while they believe themselves to be wise and performers of marvelous works, they become fools, until at length they have the master whom they serve as the hearth of both impiety and eternal exile; he attacks those dedicated to <term>Alchemy</term> in strange ways, in which the enemy of the human race sometimes so bedazzles the sight of the eyes that those practicing pyrotechnics have sworn that they have produced true gold and silver through transmutation: although...

And he says: "First, regarding mown meadows: when the grass has stopped growing and dries up in the heat, it should be cut down with scythes and turned with a fork until it is completely dry. When it has dried thoroughly, bundles should be made of it and carried to the farmhouse. Then, the stubble should be raked from the meadows and added to the haymaking pile. When this is done, the meadows should be <term>sialienda</term>—that is, cut down with scythes where the hay-mowers have missed and left the field tuberosous, as if it had a beard. I think the term 'to mow a meadow' <term>sialire pratum</term> comes from this cutting."

->L.<-

The harvest <term>messis</term> is called by this proper name in those things that are reaped, especially in grain, and it is derived from that word. There are three types of harvesting grain. One, as in Umbria, where they cut the straw close to the ground with a sickle, and place the bundle on the ground as soon as they have cut it. When they have made many of them, they count them again and cut each one between the ears and the straw, throwing the ears into a basket and sending them to the threshing floor. They leave the straw in the field to be taken to a stack. The second way they reap, as in Picenum, is where they have a curved wooden stick with an iron ferrule on the end. When this grasps a bundle of ears, it cuts them and leaves the standing straw in the field to be cut down later. The third way is reaped, as near the city of Rome and in most places, so that they cut the middle of the straw, which they grasp at the top with their left hand—from which "harvest" <term>messis</term> comes, as I think. The straw below the hand that clings to the earth is cut down afterwards. Conversely, that which clings to the straw with the ear is carried in baskets to the threshing floor, where it is winnowed in an open place <note>original: "palam"</note>—from which "chaff" <term>palea</term> can be named. Others think that "straw" <term>stramen</term> is said from "standing" <term>stando</term>. Others think it is from "bedding" <term>stratu</term>, because it is spread under cattle. When the crop is mature, it must be reaped. When about one day's work has been reaped on an acre, it is said that it is enough in a field that is easy. So they must carry the reaped ears to the threshing floor in baskets.

->LI.<-

The threshing floor should be in the field, in a higher place where the wind can blow through it. It should be moderate in size according to the size of the crop, preferably round, and slightly convex in the middle (so that if it rains, the water does not stand, but can flow down out of the threshing floor by the shortest route. Moreover, everything is shortest in a circle from the center to the edge). It should be paved with solid earth, especially if it is clay, so that it does not crack in the heat, lest grains hide in its cracks, receive water, and open doors to mice and ants. <meta>This page continues Robert Fludd’s exploration of the "Internal Monochord." It moves from the physical description of the regions of the body to the mathematical and metaphysical principles of harmony that bind the soul (unity) to the body (multiplicity).</meta>

->ON THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL HARMONY OF MAN, 247<-

...it lacks both a beginning and an end, because duality <note>original: "dualitas." In Fludd's philosophy, the number 2 represents division and the fall into matter.</note> possesses no middle point; from this, all discords—the daughters of darkness—are produced. But in truth, concords, which are the offspring of light and truth, arise from the perfect and the odd numbers.

Hence it happens that if the unity of light, which is the soul, is joined with the duality of matter, it produces an odd number, which is full of harmony. Likewise, if the trinity of the soul (which is the same in essence as unity) is added to the quaternary <note>The number four, representing the four elements of the material body.</note> of matter, it produces the number seven <note>original: "septenarium."</note>. In this number, a most perfect consonance is heard, which contains within itself the **Perfect Fifth** <term>Diapente: A musical interval of a fifth.</term> and the **Perfect Fourth** <term>Diatessaron: A musical interval of a fourth.</term>.

Consequently, this union of the soul with the body now renders that which was previously dissonant into a wondrous consonance. It makes regular, I say, that which was previously and by its own nature rebellious, irregular, and entirely opposed to motion or action. From this we find that man is nothing other than a unity and a multitude gathered together in admirable harmony.

Thus we see that just as there is but one Sun of the world, there is but one soul; yet its rays are diverse—indeed, infinite—and these rays are shared by the soul. So also we observe that all rays of light are derived from the one **Jehovah**, as if from the **Father of Lights** <note>A reference to the Biblical Epistle of James 1:17: "Every good gift... cometh down from the Father of lights."</note>, which is to say, from a single source or supersubstantial essence. His rays, flowing from Him both mediately and immediately, are in no way divided, but are rather connected in the same way that light is connected to the body of the Sun—light which is nonetheless recognized to be present in the earth, the waters, the air, and all compound things.

For this reason, the soul is called "One" because of its indivisibility from its primary form; likewise, matter is called "Multitude" because of its duality or quaternarity, which consists of a multitude or number of units. Yet for matter, an imperfect number is the principle, rather than unity. This is the reason why Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who believed that the universe was built on mathematical ratios and that a divine spirit permeated all things.</note> were of the opinion that all things are full of Gods; they referred all of these back to the one Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>, just as one refers a multitude back to unity.

But to return to this human music of ours: we have composed it from three strings and three instruments joined together, bringing forth three parts of melody. Each string and each instrument corresponds to a specific region of the world. However, because the two higher strings—namely the spiritual and the formal—coincide equally with the harmony of the string on the lowest instrument, we see it just as in the music of various melodies: the **Bass** part mingles with the **Mean** <note>The middle voice or tenor.</note>, the Mean with the **Alto**, and the Alto with the lowest parts in an equal arrangement of melodies. In this way, a multiform harmony is found within a single consensus.

Therefore, we have attributed seven keys to each triangle or pyramid, differing from one another in double or quadruple proportion. From their consonance and mutual relation to one another, we can very easily conceive and perceive the symphonic composition of the internal man with the external man.
